title: Intracranial Pressure Dynamics, Monro-Kellie Doctrine, and Cushing Triad

steps.tx: Understanding intracranial pressure dynamics requires appreciation of the physical constraints of the skull. Formulated over two centuries ago, the **Monro-Kellie doctrine** states that the rigid, non-compliant adult cranial vault represents a closed box with a fixed total internal volume. This volume comprises three physiological constituents: brain parenchyma accounting for eighty percent, cerebrospinal fluid representing ten percent, and intravascular blood comprising ten percent. Because the skull cannot expand, the sum of these volumes must remain strictly constant.
steps.say: The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that the rigid skull contains a fixed volume of brain, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid. An increase in one component requires a compensatory reduction in others.

vis.alt: Diagram illustrating intracranial compartments and intracranial pressure curves.
vis.caption: The Monro-Kellie doctrine: volumetric compensation and intracranial elastance curves. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: When a pathological mass such as an expanding traumatic haematoma develops, initial spatial compensation occurs through the displacement of cerebrospinal fluid into the distensible spinal subarachnoid space and compression of intracranial venous sinuses. During this compensated phase, large volumetric additions produce negligible changes in pressure. However, once these finite spatial buffers are exhausted, the intracranial system enters an uncompensated state characterized by high **elastance**, where even minute volumetric additions cause steep, exponential spikes in intracranial pressure.
steps.say: Early spatial compensation displaces cerebrospinal fluid and venous blood into the spinal axis. Once these buffers are exhausted, even small increases in volume cause steep, dangerous spikes in intracranial pressure.

left.title: Compensated State
points: Displacement of CSF into spinal theca

right.title: Uncompensated State
points: Precipitous drop in cerebral blood flow

steps.tx: Normal intracranial pressure in healthy supine adults ranges between five and fifteen millimetres of mercury. Pathological intracranial hypertension is defined as sustained pressure exceeding twenty millimetres of mercury, a critical threshold that impairs cerebral perfusion. Sustained intracranial pressure above this level compresses cerebral capillaries, precipitating global cerebral ischaemia. Adequate brain oxygenation depends on maintaining **cerebral perfusion pressure**, calculated mathematically as mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure, with guidelines recommending maintaining perfusion between sixty and seventy millimetres of mercury.
steps.say: Normal intracranial pressure ranges from five to fifteen millimetres of mercury. Pressures exceeding twenty require intervention to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure between sixty and seventy.

rows: Inadequate driving pressure for brain tissue

steps.tx: When critical intracranial hypertension compromises perfusion to the medullary cardiovascular centres, the brain initiates a life-saving physiological reflex. Described by Harvey Cushing, the classic **Cushing triad** represents a late, pre-terminal clinical manifestation of critically elevated intracranial pressure and brainstem distortion. The triad comprises progressive systolic hypertension with widening pulse pressure, reflex bradycardia, and irregular, depressed respirations. Recognizing this ominous triad demands instantaneous emergency interventions to prevent fatal transtentorial or tonsillar herniation.
steps.say: The Cushing triad is a late sign of brainstem compression marked by systolic hypertension with widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular respirations. It warns of imminent, fatal brain herniation.

rows: Progressive rise in systolic BP with wide pulse pressure
Massive sympathetic discharge to overcome elevated ICP
Heart rate slowing below 60 beats per minute
Carotid sinus baroreceptor response to severe hypertension
Direct compressive distortion of medullary respiratory centres

steps.tx: Uncontrolled supratentorial intracranial hypertension forces cerebral tissue through rigid anatomical apertures, precipitating life-threatening brain herniation syndromes. Expanding temporal lobe masses displace the medial parahippocampal gyrus and uncus over the sharp tentorial edge, causing **uncal herniation**. The herniating uncus directly compresses the adjacent ipsilateral oculomotor nerve, producing an unreactive, fixed dilated pupil, while compression of the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle produces contralateral motor hemiparesis. Progressive descent compresses the midbrain reticular activating system, plunging the patient into unarousable coma.
steps.say: Uncal herniation occurs when the expanding temporal lobe herniates across the tentorial edge, compressing the oculomotor nerve and brainstem. This produces a fixed dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis.

vis.alt: Medical diagram illustrating intracranial herniation syndromes and mass effect.
vis.caption: Anatomical progression of uncal and transtentorial brain herniation under severe intracranial hypertension. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Medical stabilization of acute intracranial hypertension utilizes tiered therapeutic measures designed to reduce brain volume and improve venous drainage. First-tier interventions include elevating the head of the bed to thirty degrees, maintaining the neck strictly midline to avoid internal jugular venous compression, and administering adequate analgesia. Intravenous osmotic therapy using **mannitol** at doses of zero point five to one gram per kilogram, or three percent hypertonic saline, draws free water across the intact blood-brain barrier into the intravascular space.
steps.say: First-line medical management of high intracranial pressure includes thirty-degree head elevation and osmotic therapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline to draw fluid out of swollen brain tissue.

nodes.label: Elevate Head 30 Degrees & Keep Neck Midline
Administer IV Mannitol or 3% Hypertonic Saline

steps.tx: Controlled mechanical hyperventilation serves as a temporary emergency rescue bridge when herniation is imminent. Lowering arterial carbon dioxide tension to thirty to thirty-five millimetres of mercury induces rapid cerebral **arteriolar vasoconstriction**, reducing cerebral blood volume and rapidly lowering intracranial pressure. However, prolonged or aggressive hyperventilation dropping arterial carbon dioxide below thirty millimetres of mercury is strictly avoided because intense vasoconstriction precipitates severe secondary cerebral ischaemia and infarction in vulnerable penumbral brain regions.
steps.say: Brief hyperventilation rapidly lowers intracranial pressure by inducing cerebral vasoconstriction. It must be used only as a temporary bridge, as severe vasoconstriction causes cerebral ischaemia.

left.title: Controlled Mild Hyperventilation
points: Used as acute bridge to definitive therapy

right.title: Aggressive Hyperventilation
points: Strictly avoided in acute brain trauma

steps.tx: When medical resuscitation fails to arrest rapid uncal herniation and a neurosurgical operating suite is unavailable, emergency surgical decompression is life-saving. In peripheral facilities, an emergency **exploratory burr hole** or trephination is placed two centimetres anterior and three centimetres superior to the external auditory meatus on the side of the dilated pupil. Evacuating an acute extradural haematoma decompresses the brainstem, after which the patient is transferred immediately to a tertiary neurosurgical center for definitive formal craniotomy.
steps.say: In rapidly deteriorating patients when transfer is delayed, an emergency exploratory burr hole on the side of the dilated pupil can release an extradural clot and save the patient's life.

nodes.label: Blown Pupil and Impending Brainstem Death
Identify Site (2 cm Anterior, 3 cm Superior to Tragus)
Evacuate Clot and Transfer for Definitive Craniotomy
